claims.text: Sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane initially exhibit a single-phase FCC structure.
The initial nanoparticle population contains elliptical and icosahedral geometries.
Above approximately 0.45 times the weighted-average melting temperature, sluggish diffusion is overridden in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Surface-energy minimization drives Au and Cu to migrate rapidly to nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface enrichment of Au and Cu creates a concentration gradient that promotes their evaporation.
Evaporation of surface-enriched Au and Cu leads to Ostwald ripening.
The elemental surface energies follow the ordering γ_Au < γ_Cu < γ_Ni < γ_Co < γ_Pt.
Au and Cu segregation produces a core-shell-like composition gradient.
The core-shell-like composition gradient lowers the activation energy for surface diffusion and evaporation.
Above the critical temperature, the surface-energy driving force exceeds the kinetic barrier associated with lattice distortion.
Au and Cu have lower cohesive energies than Pt, Co, and Ni and therefore evaporate preferentially.
Preferential Au and Cu evaporation leaves refractory-element-rich particle cores.
The remaining refractory-rich cores subsequently shrink and coalesce.
At approximately 0.45 Tm, the rate of Au and Cu surface enrichment accelerates nonlinearly.
Surface segregation and evaporation cause measurable mass loss from particles smaller than 5 nm.
The particle-size distribution shifts toward larger, refractory-rich particles during heating.
Icosahedral particles have higher surface energy and lose Au and Cu faster than truncated-octahedral particles.
The proposed mechanism applies only to particles smaller than 10 nm because of their high surface-to-volume ratio.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion dominates and the surface-driven mechanism does not apply.
Higher environmental pressure may suppress evaporation of surface-enriched elements.

contradictions.description: The proposed mechanism requires rapid Au and Cu surface diffusion, but the key simulation is described as artificially suppressing diffusion with high activation barriers while still allowing surface-energy minimization. Surface-energy-driven segregation itself requires atomic transport, so observing the proposed mediator under a genuinely diffusion-suppressed constraint is internally inconsistent.

The rule treats agreement with a diffusion-suppressed model and agreement with a fast-diffusion model as equivalent grounds for rejection of sluggish diffusion, although these alternatives make opposing assumptions about the required atomic mobility. It therefore does not provide a unique decisive test of the proposed surface-diffusion mechanism.
